how.title: How an AI agent actually works
how.lede: A chatbot answers a question. An agent finishes a job. It reads your data, decides what to do, uses your tools to do it, and checks the result before anyone relies on it. Each turn of that loop is logged.

loop.title: Read
loop.description: The agent collects what it needs from the systems you allowed: the inbox, the ledger, the ticket queue, the repository. It sees only what its permissions allow.

loop.title: Reason
loop.description: A large language model works out what the job needs and plans the steps. This is the only place intelligence is used, so it is spent where judgement matters.

loop.title: Act
loop.description: The agent uses real tools through connectors and MCP servers: it drafts the reply, files the report, raises the pull request. Rule-based steps stay as plain code.

loop.title: Check
loop.description: Before anything is sent, spent or deleted the agent stops at an approval gate. You approve, or reject with a reason it learns from. Every step is traced.

how.layersTitle: Three layers in every agent we build

layers.title: The model

shoes.title: We get into your shoes first
shoes.lede: Most AI projects fail because they automate the wrong step. Our forward deployed engineers sit with the people who do the work before writing a line of code.

steps.title: Shadow the work
steps.description: We watch a real working day: the inbox, the approvals, the spreadsheets that hold the business together. We note every hand-off and every wait.

steps.title: Map the data sources
steps.description: For each step we record where the data lives, who owns it, how it is reached (API, export, database, email) and how sensitive it is.

steps.title: Find where judgement is needed
steps.description: We split each process into rule steps, which stay as ordinary automation, and judgement steps, where an LLM earns its cost. Agents go only where intelligence is required.

steps.title: Build and run beside you
steps.description: The first agent runs on your real data with an approval gate on every risky action. We tune it with the people who use it, then widen its permissions only when they trust it.

journey.title: Tell us about your business
journey.lede: These are the questions we ask in the first customer meeting. Your answers stay in your browser until you choose to send them.
journey.summaryEmpty: Your blueprint builds here as you answer.

questions.title: Who is the agent working for first?
questions.help: We start with one person or team. The quickest wins are usually the people whose time is most expensive.

options.label: CEO or founder
options.description: Inbox, diary, board packs, investor updates

questions.title: Where does the time go today?
questions.help: Pick the work that is repetitive but still needs someone to think. That is where an agent pays for itself.

options.label: Email and diary
options.description: Triage, replies, meeting scheduling and preparation

options.label: Reports and briefings
options.description: Board packs, weekly updates, KPI commentary

options.label: Data entry between systems
options.description: Copying from email or PDF into CRM, ERP or spreadsheets

questions.title: Where does the data live?
questions.help: This is the first thing an FDE maps in a meeting. Every source becomes a connector with its own permissions.

options.label: Files and scans
options.description: PDFs, spreadsheets, scanned forms, file shares

options.label: In-house or legacy systems
options.description: Custom apps, old APIs, screens with no API

questions.title: How much should the agent do on its own?
questions.help: We always start with more approval and loosen it as trust grows. You can change this per agent and per tool.

options.label: Draft only
options.description: It prepares everything; a person sends, pays or posts

options.label: Act on low risk, ask on high risk
options.description: Reads and drafts run alone; sending, spending and deleting wait for approval

options.label: Run on its own within limits
options.description: Budgets, allow-lists and stop conditions; people review the log

questions.title: Which AI company would you like to work with?
questions.help: Our engineers are certified across all the major platforms, so this is your choice, not ours. If you have no preference we choose per task.

options.label: Anthropic Claude
options.description: Strong at long documents, careful reasoning, tool use and code

options.label: OpenAI
options.description: GPT models, broad ecosystem, voice and vision

options.label: Google Gemini
options.description: Long context, multimodal, close to Google Workspace

options.label: Microsoft
options.description: Azure OpenAI and Copilot inside your Microsoft tenant

options.label: No preference
options.description: Choose the best model for each agent

questions.title: Would you prefer open-source models?
questions.help: Open-weight models such as Llama, Qwen, Mistral, DeepSeek and gpt-oss can run on your own hardware, with no per-token bill and no data leaving your network.

options.label: Yes, open source first
options.description: Use open-weight models wherever they are good enough

options.label: A mix
options.description: Open source for routine or sensitive work, a frontier model for the hardest steps

options.label: No, use the best commercial model
options.description: Quality first; open source is not a requirement

questions.title: Where should the AI run?
questions.help: This decides which models are possible. A fully offline system needs open-weight models on your own AI workstations.

options.label: Provider cloud API
options.description: Fastest to start; data covered by the provider's enterprise terms

options.label: Our own cloud tenant
options.description: Azure, AWS or Google Cloud account we control, UK or EU region

options.label: Self-hosted, on our premises
options.description: Our own servers or AI workstations, still connected to the internet

options.label: Self-hosted and offline
options.description: AI workstations with no internet connection at all

questions.title: What kind of data will the agent touch?
questions.help: This sets the guardrails: redaction, where logs are kept and who can approve what.

options.label: Personal data
options.description: Customers, staff or patients under UK GDPR

result.summaryHeading: AI agent blueprint from the TenthMatrix journey

ceo.name: Executive PA agent
ceo.description: Triages the CEO's inbox overnight, drafts replies in their voice, prepares a one-page brief before every meeting and turns board-pack data into a first draft of the chair's update.

cto.name: Engineering PA agent
cto.description: Reviews pull requests against your standards, summarises overnight incidents with likely causes, and writes the weekly engineering status from GitHub and Jira so the CTO reads, not compiles.

cfo.name: Finance PA agent
cfo.description: Drafts month-end variance commentary from the ledger, checks invoices and purchase orders against policy before they reach the CFO, and keeps a rolling cash briefing up to date.

coo.name: Operations agent
coo.description: Watches orders, supplier emails and schedules for exceptions, chases late deliveries with a drafted message, and escalates only what needs a decision.

sales.name: Pipeline agent
sales.description: Researches every new lead, drafts the first reply and proposal, updates the CRM from email threads and flags deals that have gone quiet.

support.name: Customer service agent
support.description: Classifies every ticket, answers routine questions from your knowledge base, drafts replies for the rest and routes complaints and refunds to the right person.

people.name: People team agent
people.description: Screens applications against the role, schedules interviews, prepares onboarding packs and answers policy questions from your handbook with a citation.

legal.name: Contracts and compliance agent
legal.description: Reads incoming contracts, compares them to your playbook, highlights non-standard clauses with a suggested redline and keeps an evidence log for audits.

default.name: Business PA agent
default.description: Takes the repetitive, judgement-heavy work off your busiest people, starting with the process we agree in discovery.

inbox.name: Mail agent
inbox.description: Watches chosen senders, researches the thread and leaves a reply draft for approval.

reporting.name: Briefing agent
reporting.description: Pulls the numbers on a schedule and writes the commentary, citing where each figure came from.

approvals.name: Approvals agent
approvals.description: Checks each request against policy and budget, then routes it with a recommendation.

customers.name: Enquiry agent
customers.description: Answers routine questions, drafts quotes and follows up until the customer replies.

documents.name: Document agent
documents.description: Extracts, compares and summarises contracts, reports and forms into structured data.

engineering.name: PR review and incident agent
engineering.description: Reviews pull requests and turns alerts and logs into a readable incident summary.

research.name: Research agent
research.description: Returns cited findings you can open: competitors, suppliers, markets and due diligence.

data.name: Data entry agent
data.description: Reads emails and PDFs and writes the fields into your CRM, ERP or spreadsheet, with a check before saving.

anthropic.name: Anthropic Claude
anthropic.why: Careful reasoning over long documents and reliable tool use; our first choice for agents that write code or handle complex workflows.

openai.name: OpenAI GPT
openai.why: A broad ecosystem with strong general reasoning, vision and voice for customer-facing agents.

google.name: Google Gemini
google.why: Very long context and multimodal input, and close to the data if you run on Google Workspace.

microsoft.name: Azure OpenAI in your Microsoft tenant
microsoft.why: OpenAI models under your Microsoft agreement and data boundary, alongside Copilot and Microsoft 365 permissions.

xai.name: xAI Grok
xai.why: Fast reasoning with real-time knowledge, useful for research and market-watching agents.

open.name: Open-weight models (Llama, Qwen, Mistral, DeepSeek, gpt-oss)
open.why: Run on your own hardware through vLLM or Ollama: no per-token bill and no data leaving your network.

openRoutine.name: A small open-weight model for routine steps
openRoutine.why: Classification, extraction and redaction run locally and cheaply; only the hardest steps go to the frontier model.

hosting.cloud: The provider's enterprise API, with zero data retention where it is offered. Fastest to start; we can move to your own tenant later without rebuilding the agents.
hosting.tenant: Your own Azure, AWS or Google Cloud account in a UK or EU region. Models are reached through your cloud's private endpoints, and logs stay in your account.
hosting.onprem: Self-hosted on your own servers or AI workstations. Jobshout, the models and the logs run inside your network; we connect only to the services you allow.
hosting.airgap: Fully offline on AI workstations with no internet connection. Open-weight models run locally, updates arrive on approved media, and nothing leaves the building.

recommend.airgapNote: Cloud models from {provider} need an internet connection, so for an offline system we would use open-weight models locally and keep {provider} for any connected work you add later.

connectors.m365: Microsoft Graph connector (mail, calendar, Teams, SharePoint) with delegated permissions
connectors.google: Google Workspace connector (Gmail, Calendar, Drive) scoped per user
connectors.crm: CRM connector reading and updating records, with writes behind approval
connectors.finance: Finance connector with read access to the ledger; postings and payments always approved
connectors.dev: GitHub, GitLab and Jira connectors through MCP
connectors.helpdesk: Help desk connector for tickets, macros and knowledge base
connectors.chat: Slack or Teams bot so people brief and approve agents where they already work
connectors.database: Read-only database or warehouse connector with row-level permissions
connectors.files: Document pipeline with OCR for PDFs, scans and spreadsheets
connectors.legacy: Custom MCP server or browser automation for systems with no usable API

controls.draft: Draft-only mode: the agent never sends, pays or posts; a person does.
controls.gated: Approval gates on every send, spend, post or delete. Reads and drafts run on their own.
controls.auto: Autonomous within budgets, allow-lists and stop conditions, with a daily review of the run log.
controls.always: Every step, input, output, token count and cost is traced and kept for audit.
controls.personal: Personal data is redacted before it reaches any model outside your boundary.
controls.financial: Payments and ledger postings always need a named approver.
controls.health: Special category data stays on infrastructure you control, with access logged per record.
controls.privileged: Privileged and board documents stay in a separate workspace with its own approvers.
controls.ip: Source code is processed under zero-retention terms or on self-hosted models only.

now: Week 1: discovery on site, shadowing the work and mapping the data sources
Week 2: first agent live on your real data with approval gates
Weeks 3–4: tune with the people who use it, then widen permissions
quarter: Weeks 1–2: discovery across the teams and a ranked list of agents
Weeks 3–6: first two agents live, connectors hardened
Weeks 7–12: rollout, training and handover to your team

A written business case with costs, savings and risks per agent
A two-week pilot on the process with the clearest return

scenarios.ceo: It is 7:30. Before the CEO opens the laptop, the Executive PA agent has read 140 overnight emails, archived the noise, drafted 11 replies in their voice and put a one-page brief on top: the three decisions needed today, the investor who is waiting on numbers, and the notes for the 10:00 board call. The CEO approves eight replies from their phone and edits three.
scenarios.cto: A deployment failed at 02:14. By 08:00 the Engineering PA agent has collected the logs, linked the failing commit, written an incident summary with a likely cause and opened a draft fix as a pull request. The on-call engineer reviews it instead of starting from scratch.
scenarios.cfo: On working day two of month-end, the Finance PA agent has reconciled the bank feed, drafted variance commentary for every cost centre that moved more than 5% and listed the four invoices that break purchasing policy. The CFO spends an hour reviewing instead of three days compiling.
scenarios.coo: A supplier emails that a shipment will be a week late. The Operations agent finds the affected orders, drafts a message to the three customers involved and proposes an alternative supplier from your approved list. The operations manager approves two messages and phones the third customer.
scenarios.sales: A new enquiry arrives at 18:00. The Pipeline agent researches the company, scores the fit, drafts a reply with a relevant case study and books a slot in the account manager's diary for approval. The lead hears back the same evening.
scenarios.support: On a Monday morning 300 tickets are waiting. The Customer service agent has answered 180 routine ones from the knowledge base, drafted replies for 90 and flagged 30 complaints for a person, sorted by risk of churn.
scenarios.people: A role attracts 400 applications. The People team agent screens them against the criteria, shortlists 25 with reasons, schedules first interviews and sends every other applicant a courteous reply for approval.
scenarios.legal: A customer sends back a 40-page contract. The Contracts and compliance agent compares it to your playbook, highlights six non-standard clauses, suggests a redline for each and records the review in the evidence log.
scenarios.default: An FDE spends a day with your team, finds the process that eats the most expensive hours, and has an agent doing the first draft of it on your real data within two weeks.

items.title: "I spend my first two hours every day on email."
items.description: The FDE mapped Outlook, the CRM and the board portal, and found that most replies followed five patterns. An Executive PA agent now drafts replies and meeting briefs overnight; the CEO approves from a phone.

items.title: "Month-end takes nine days and most of it is copying."
items.description: Discovery showed the judgement was only in the variance commentary; matching and posting were rules. We automated the rules in code and put an agent on the commentary and the policy checks.
list: Data: Sage, bank feeds, purchase order spreadsheets
Model: a mix of a local model for extraction and a frontier model for commentary
Control: no posting or payment without a named approver

items.title: "My senior engineers spend their week reviewing other people's code."
items.description: A PR review agent checks every pull request against the team's standards and a second agent writes incident summaries from Sentry and logs. Seniors review the agent's notes, not the whole diff.
list: Model: Claude Code for review, with an open-weight model for log triage
Control: comments only; merging stays human

items.title: "Nothing privileged can ever leave the building."
items.description: We sized AI workstations with Workstation and ran open-weight models fully offline. A contracts agent compares documents to the firm's playbook and drafts redlines; partners approve each one.
list: Data: document management system, precedent bank
Model: open-weight models on local GPU workstations
Control: air-gapped, with audit logs kept on site

offline.title: Want your AI with no internet connection at all?
offline.body: Some data can never leave the building. We run open-weight models on AI workstations inside your network, fully offline, and build the same agents on top. The hardware comes from our sister company Workstation.

items.question: What is the difference between a chatbot and an AI agent?
items.answer: A chatbot answers. An agent completes a task: it reads your systems, plans, uses tools to do the work and stops for approval before anything risky. You get a finished draft, report or update, not a paragraph of advice.

items.question: Do we have to choose one AI company?
items.answer: No. Many of our clients use a frontier model for the hardest steps and a small open-weight model for routine ones. Jobshout lets each agent use a different model, and you can switch later without rebuilding.

items.question: Can the agents run without any internet connection?
items.answer: Yes. With open-weight models on AI workstations from Workstation, the whole system, including the models, the framework and the logs, runs offline inside your building.

items.question: What does a forward deployed engineer actually do?
items.answer: They sit with your team, map your processes and data sources, decide where an LLM is worth using, and build and deploy the agents in your environment. They stay until the people who use the agent trust it.

items.question: What happens to the answers I give in this journey?
items.answer: Nothing, until you press send. The blueprint is worked out in your browser. If you send it, it reaches our team as an enquiry so an engineer can prepare for the first meeting.
